sentences.text: It is also a bread and butter issue that has implications for the business competitiveness and economic viability of our nation Over the past decade, there has in fact been an erosion in the rule of law worldwide for which Singapore has sadly not been exempt because the success of the rule of law relies on the confidence of those who participate in it.

sections.label: World Justice Project rule of law
sections.summary: According to the World Justice Project, cited by Ms Sylvia Lim, adherence to the rule of law has fallen for the third consecutive year since 2017.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: According to the World Justice Project, which my colleague Ms Sylvia Lim, cited earlier on, adherence to the rule of law has fallen for the third consecutive year since 2017.

sections.label: Justice quality and judicial independence scores
sections.summary: The World Justice Project's civil and criminal justice quality scores fell to their lowest since 2012, and judicial independence slid from its 2008 peak.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: The World Justice Project's assessments of the quality of civil and criminal justice fell to the lowest it has ever been since scores were first compiled in 2012.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Our judicial independence as adjudged by the World Economic Forum continues to slide from its peak in 2008.

sections.label: Rule of law and investment
sections.summary: Deteriorations in the rule of law affect domestic and foreign investment activity, productivity and growth.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Deteriorations in the rule of law affect in particular domestic as well as foreign investment activity, as well as productivity and growth.

sections.label: Rule of law and economic outcomes
sections.summary: North Korea was more prosperous at partition but Seoul now outproduces it, with the rule of law cited as a major factor.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: What many of us may be less familiar with is that at the time of partition, it was North Korea that was the more prosperous half, the more industrialised part of the peninsula.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Yet today, the city of Seoul itself produces more than 10 times the economic product of the entire economy of North Korea.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: There are, of course, many reasons for the ultimate difference in economic outcomes of the two regions, but one major factor was that the North chose to pursue an institutional path that failed to respect the importance of the rule of law while the South continued to do so.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: So, when we flag concerns of fairness, excess and independence in Singapore's justice system, we are not merely talking about the alleged judicial missteps of the Parti Liyani case or about other cases of potential lapses in the fairness of the justice system, which my colleagues have mentioned.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: It is also about the divergent fortunes of the Nogales and Koreas of the world.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: And when we underscore the importance of the rule of law, we are not only trafficking in the realm of our shared notions of justice, but our common economic future as well.

sections.label: Appropriate Adult Scheme for foreign domestic workers
sections.summary: The speaker asks the Government to reconsider including foreign domestic workers under the Appropriate Adult Scheme.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: My first point is about the Appropriate Adult Scheme that I raised in my Parliamentary Question that Minister addressed earlier.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: But can I appeal to the Government to re-consider and include foreign domestic workers for a start under this scheme and not all work permit holders?

sections.label: Video recording timeline and interpreters
sections.summary: The speaker asks MHA for the timeline for full video recording implementation and for interpreters in suspects' own language.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: All I am asking is whether MHA could share the timeline for the full implementation of this video recording.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Can we ensure that all suspects are provided an interpreter in their own language and not just in a language that they understand, which the Minister has mentioned earlier?

sections.label: Interpreter in own language
sections.summary: The suspect should be provided an interpreter in their own language.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Second, the suspect should be provided an interpreter in their own language.

sections.label: Interpreter present before police interviews
sections.summary: Police interviews should not start unless the interpreter is in the room.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Fifth, Police interviews should not start unless the interpreter is in the room.

sections.label: Singapore ranking versus Ombudsman countries
sections.summary: Singapore ranked 12th in 2020 and scored 97 in the Gallup Law and Order survey, ahead of Indonesia, Malaysia and the Philippines.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: Singapore, in 2020, was ranked 12th, an improvement from the previous year.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: In contrast, the three countries that Mr Perera cited as having had Ombudsman – Indonesia, Malaysia and the Philippines – were ranked 59th, 47th and 91st respectively.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: If you were to take the most recent Gallup Law and Order survey, out of a hundred points, Singapore scored 97.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: Indonesia, the Philippines and Malaysia were at least 10 points behind Singapore.

sections.label: Civil actions against Government
sections.summary: In the last two years, 46 civil actions were filed against the Government.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: And I thought I heard Mr Perera said that it is very difficult to bring an action in Court, either by way of judicial review or otherwise.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: I had a quick look at the numbers and, in the last two years, there were 46 civil actions filed against the Government.

sections.label: Charges and trial dates for Liyani
sections.summary: AGC directed charges against Ms Liyani, she was charged on 31 August 2017, and AGC asked for February 2018 trial dates.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: Eventually, on 10 August 2017, the AGC directed the Police to prefer charges against Ms Liyani.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: She was charged in Court on 31 August 2017 and released on bail.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: Ms Liyani claimed trial to the charges and, at the second pre-trial conference in October 2017, AGC asked for trial dates in February 2018 – four months later.

sections.label: Hearing length, witnesses and pages
sections.summary: The hearing concluded on 17 January 2019 over 20 hearing days, with 16 witnesses and 3,699 pages of proceedings.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: Due to the issues, it could not be concluded within the allocated period, and it took place over several tranches and eventually concluded on 17 January 2019 – 20 hearing days.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: And we are not suggesting for a moment, I think, that we should truncate the trial simply because we want to have speed as opposed to thoroughness.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: There was a total of 16 witnesses – 12 prosecution witnesses, four defence witnesses – and the record of proceedings came up to 3,699 pages.

sections.label: High Court acquits Ms Liyani
sections.summary: After submissions heard over three days, the High Court acquitted Ms Liyani on 4 September 2020.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: Detailed submissions were put forward to the High Court by both parties, and this was heard over three days – in November 2019, February 2020 and August 2020 and, eventually, the High Court acquitted Ms Liyani on 4 September 2020.

sections.label: QSM, ombudsman systems and context
sections.summary: QSM is not independent of the authority complained about, and the speaker says other countries' ombudsman outcomes do not fare better than Singapore's own systems.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: QSM is not an independent process that is outside of the authorities, Statutory Board or Ministry that is the subject of the complaint.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: Meet-the-People sessions do not include an independent fact-finding process.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: I am not generalising and I know that you have gone into a series of other countries.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: I think if you did the research – which I am sure you did – you would have seen numerous articles about the ombudsman system in Australia, in the UK and the failings that they have had.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Second, I am not in a position to speculate as to what might happen to those countries were there no ombudsman.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: But I think the point I am making is two-fold: first, look at the outcome in these countries – I am suggesting that they do not fare better than Singapore and I am sure the Member will agree; and second, perhaps more importantly, that we have our own systems, we have our own context.

sections.label: QSM and complaint avenues
sections.summary: The speaker says an ombudsman is not needed for rudeness, citing the QSM, MPs and REACH as avenues.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: On his third point about the QSM, I made the point in response to the fact that you do not need an ombudsman to deal with someone who is rude to an individual.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: That is where you have the QSM, you have your Members of Parliament, you have other avenues like REACH to deal with.

sections.label: Ms Liyani public concerns
sections.summary: Ms Liyani's case raised public questions on officer compliance, investigation procedures and the trial judge's qualifications, which Minister Shanmugam addressed.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
sentences.text: Ms Liyani's case has sparked questions from the public on whether individual law enforcement officers have complied with the standard operating procedures, whether there are flaws in the investigation procedures of the Attorney-General's Chambers, and the qualifications of the trial judge.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
sentences.text: In the Ministerial Statement by Minister K Shanmugam earlier, he addressed these concerns by setting out the facts and the corresponding remedial actions.

sections.label: Criminal Legal Aid Scheme funding
sections.summary: The government funds CLAS, which aided Ms Liyani, allocating about $2 million yearly from 2015 to 2019 and taking up close to 1,000 cases.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
sentences.text: The Singapore government's stand on this issue is clear: we seek a fair and just democratic society and will never tolerate the formation of closed circles of elites.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
sentences.text: This includes providing pro-bono legal advice and representation to those who have limited means through the Criminal Legal Aid Scheme (CLAS).

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
sentences.text: Ms Liyani is one such beneficiary under this Scheme.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
sentences.text: From 2015 to 2019, the government allocated an average of $2 million per year to fund the scheme.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
sentences.text: Over the past 4 years, they have taken up close to 1,000 cases, ensuring that no Singaporean will be denied the help they need because they cannot afford to pay for a lawyer.

sections.label: Law enforcement and safety ranking
sections.summary: Law enforcement agencies have pledged allegiance for up to 200 years, and Singapore ranked second in the world's safest cities.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
sentences.text: Our law enforcement agencies have pledged allegiance to the country and to protect people's lives and property for up to 200 years.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
sentences.text: We are proud that Singapore ranked second in the world's safest cities, just behind Tokyo.

sections.label: Separation of powers independence
sections.summary: The separation of powers ensures independence of the Legislature, Executive and Judiciary, so even powerful persons may face independent trials and CPIB investigations.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
sentences.text: The separation of powers is the cornerstone of our democratic system and ensures the independence of the Legislature, the Executive and the Judiciary branches of Government.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
sentences.text: Hence, even for someone who has power in the Executive or Legislative branches of Government, he may still be tried independently before the law by the Judiciary branch of Government, and may still be subject to independent investigations by the Corrupt Practices Investigation Bureau.

sections.label: Three pillars since independence
sections.summary: Since independence the Government has upheld accountability, fairness, equality and separation of powers, building the nation promised in the Pledge.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
sentences.text: Since Singapore's independence, the Government has upheld the three pillars of accountability, fairness and equality, and the separation of powers, and in so doing, built the progressive, prosperous, just, and equal nation, that we have today, just as promised in our Pledge.

sections.label: Employer duties for foreign domestic workers
sections.summary: The Employment of Foreign Manpower Act requires employers to pay domestic workers timely and in full and upkeep their maintenance in Singapore.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
sentences.text: Under the Employment of Foreign Manpower Act and Regulations, employers are required to make timely and full payment of salary to their domestic workers and help upkeep their maintenance during their employment in Singapore.

sections.label: Amendments on rest days and insurance
sections.summary: Amendments required weekly rest days or compensation in 2013, accident insurance of $60,000 in 2018, and no safekeeping of salaries in 2019.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
sentences.text: In 2013, the law was amended to require employers to provide foreign domestic workers with weekly rest day or compensation in lieu.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
sentences.text: In 2018, employers were required to purchase personal accident insurance with payout of $60,000, up from $40,000 previously, for their foreign domestic workers.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
sentences.text: More recently in 2019, the law was amended to explicitly disallow employers from safekeeping the salary of their foreign domestic workers to reduce downstream salary disputes.

sections.label: Removal of abused domestic workers
sections.summary: Foreign domestic workers who are victims of errant employers will be removed from their employers' place of residence for protection.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
sentences.text: Foreign domestic workers who are victims of errant employers will be removed from their employers' place of residence for their protection.

sections.label: Equality before the law, judicial power
sections.summary: Article 12 requires all persons to be equal before the law, and Article 93 vests judicial power in the Supreme Court and State Courts.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: Article 12, which requires all persons to be equal before the law and be entitled to equal protection of the law.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: Article 93, which vests the judicial power in the Supreme Court in the State Courts.

sections.label: DPP disciplinary action in Parti Liyani case
sections.summary: The DPPs in the Parti Liyani case were referred for disciplinary action over possible breaches of Kadar obligations, a separate process.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: The hon Leader of Opposition referred to the fact that the DPPs in the Parti Liyani case were referred for disciplinary action in relation to whether or not they had breached the Kadar obligations.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: So, this is a separate process that will have to take place.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: And if these DPPs are held to be in breach, then they would have to suffer the consequences, while maintaining the independence of the Judiciary and the Attorney-General's office.

sections.label: Balancing victims, accused, public, state resources
sections.summary: The passage states that there can be good ideas but ultimately a balancing process is needed among victims, accused persons, the public and state resources.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: While there can be good ideas, at the end of the day, it is a balancing process.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: We need to balance the interests of the victims, the accused persons, the public and, of course, the state resources of which the Minister for Finance is in charge of.

sections.label: Arrest, charge and imprisonment
sections.summary: The person was nabbed within a few days, charged in Court, convicted and given a long imprisonment term.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: That helped us nab him within a few days.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: He was charged in Court and convicted and sentenced to a long imprisonment term.

sections.label: Serious Sexual Crime Branch
sections.summary: Rape cases moved from Division level to the Serious Sexual Crime Branch under the CID, where specially trained officers attend to sexual offence victims.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: Previously, rape cases were dealt with at the Division level.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: Now, we have the Serious Sexual Crime Branch under the CID, where Police officers are given special training to give special attention to victims of sexual offences and, in the process, make sure that they would get the justice that they deserve.

sections.label: Murder of SI Boo
sections.summary: On 30 November 1994, SI Boo was murdered along Newton Road by a person he stopped to check, who chopped him with an axe.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: In the early morning of 30 November 1994, SI Boo was murdered by a person whom he stopped to check along Newton Road.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: The person was apparently walking home after an aborted robbery attempt.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: He chopped SI Boo with an axe that he extricated from a bag he was carrying.

sections.label: Law Society pro bono culture
sections.summary: The Law Society of Singapore has nurtured a strong pro bono culture, especially through CLAS started in the 1980s by the late Mr Harry Elias.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: At this point, I wish to state that it is a matter of pride for me that over the years, the Law Society of Singapore has nurtured a strong culture of pro bono work amongst its lawyers, especially through the Criminal Legal Aid Scheme or CLAS started in the 1980s by the late Mr Harry Elias, Senior Counsel, and now supported by MinLaw.

sections.label: Bail as judicial decision
sections.summary: Responding to Ms Sylvia Lim, the provision of bail is a judicial decision.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: And this may be a convenient time for me to deal with a few points that the hon Member Ms Sylvia Lim raised in her speech.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: She pointed out that bails could work adversely for poor people because they cannot post bail.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: I wish to state that the provision of bail is a judicial decision.

sections.label: Fines as judicial punishment
sections.summary: On Ms Sylvia Lim's point about fines for indigent persons, the imposition of a fine is a punishment by the Judge acting in judicial discretion.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: Ms Sylvia Lim also mentioned about the difficulty of paying fines for indigent persons.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: And that is a fair point but again, I come back to the important note that the imposition of a fine is a punishment by the Judge acting in his judicial discretion.

sections.label: Wording on Singapore justice system
sections.summary: Proposes replacing "affirms" with "recognises" and adding race, language and religion, and deleting a review phrase.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
sentences.text: The first point is really replacing "affirms" with "recognises", to be more precise.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
sentences.text: And that is to state the fact that from the outset, from Singapore's Independence, fairness, access and independence are cornerstones of the Singapore justice system.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
sentences.text: And the next point, Sir, it is in relation to the usage of the word "affirms".

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
sentences.text: And this is really to state as a matter of truth, that the Government has been continually putting in the effort since Independence to build a fair and just society, to remedy any shortcoming to enhance justice for all regardless of race, language, religion, economic means or social status.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
sentences.text: So, I added the words "race, language, religion" and I do not think that should be controversial.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
sentences.text: I have proposed to delete "including facilitating a review" of the justice system.

sections.label: Alleged prosecutorial structure weakness
sections.summary: Mr Singh's first point was an alleged weakness from the Attorney-General's two roles as legal advisor and Public Prosecutor.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: His first point was that there is, allegedly, a weakness in our prosecutorial structure and that arises from the two roles of the AG: one being his role as the Government's legal advisor and the other being the role as a Public Prosecutor.

sections.label: Decoupling Public Prosecutor roles
sections.summary: Rejects decoupling the Public Prosecutor from the Attorney-General, saying the Executive has no say in criminal matters.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: I believe this separation exists in other countries to enhance the independence of the PP's office." So, the first point that she made was that, you must decouple it so that the person, who is the PP, is not the same person taking the Government's instructions in non-criminal matters.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: But this argument is not correct because in non-criminal matters the Attorney-General advises the Government, the Government is his client.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: And similar to private sector matters, he takes in instructions on matters which are within the Government's purview.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: But in criminal matters, the Attorney-General decides whether to prosecute.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: The Executive and the Cabinet have no say in that.

sections.label: ST Marine officers convicted 2017
sections.summary: In 2017 seven former ST Marine officers were convicted for corrupt payments and other offences.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: In 2017, seven former officers of ST Marine who had been charged were convicted for giving corrupt payments to secure business and/or for other offences.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: These officers included former Presidents of ST Marine See Leong Teck and Chang Cheow Teck.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: ST Marine is a subsidiary of ST Engineering, which is in turn, majority-owned by Temasek Holdings, which is a Government-linked company.

sections.label: Prime Minister's consultations
sections.summary: The Prime Minister does it in consultation with the Chief Justice, incumbent Attorney-General and Public Service Commission Chairman.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: The Prime Minister does it in consultation with the Chief Justice, in consultation with the incumbent Attorney-General and the Chairman of the Public Service Commission.

sections.label: Ex-MP as Public Prosecutor
sections.summary: Mr Singh's third point suggested the system eschews appointing ex-Members of Parliament as Public Prosecutors.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: The third point that Mr Singh made was that he suggested that the system eschews the appointment of ex-Member of Parliament as a Public Prosecutor.

sections.label: Former MP as Attorney-General
sections.summary: Mr Singh said a former elected MP would naturally have imbibed the political views of the party he or she represented.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: Because Ms Sylvia Lim before when she raised this point, talked about not having an ex-Member of Parliament, or MP, as the Attorney-General.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: The reason given by Mr Singh was this.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: He said firstly it would be natural for a former elected MP to have imbibed the political views of the party he or she used to represent.

sections.label: Lucien Wong recusal and appearances
sections.summary: Mr Singh said appearances matter, noting Mr Lucien Wong was not involved in prosecutorial decisions on Ms Parti Liyani and would recuse himself from any review.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: Mr Singh did point out that appearances are important, he referred to how in this case, it was mentioned that the Attorney-General Mr Lucien Wong was not involved in any prosecutorial decisions regarding Ms Parti Liyani and that he would recuse himself from any on-going review of the case.

sections.label: Conflict in Attorney-General roles
sections.summary: The speaker says the Leader's answers have not squarely addressed possible conflict between the Attorney-General as Government legal adviser and as public prosecutor.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: The first, with regard to a general point that the Leader makes about conflict.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: I will make the point that I do not believe the Leader's answers have squarely addressed the reality of possible conflict between the Attorney-General in his role as Government legal adviser on the one hand and public prosecutor on the other.

sections.label: Attorney-General term length proposal
sections.summary: The speaker says a term of at least five years would serve the Government well and agrees with Mr Walter Woon's suggestion.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: Even in our own experience in Singapore, we have had Attorney-Generals who have served for a long period of time, and others just two years.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: And my point really is, it would serve the Government well, if the term was at least, for example, five years.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: I can agree with the suggestion that Mr Walter Woon made because it heightens the prospect of independence in the eyes of the public that this individual was not removed for reasons which the public may start imagining – which may or may not be true.

sections.label: Public view on party ties
sections.summary: The speaker says the bigger question is whether the public see it that way and that it is probably more propitious for the individual not to be associated with a political party.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: But again, I think the bigger question is whether the public see it that way.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: And I would forward that while reasonable people can have different views about this, it is probably more propitious to have that individual not be associated with a political party.

sections.label: Keppel O&M conditional warning case
sections.summary: The speaker says a conditional warning with penalties was issued to the company in the Keppel O&M case and evidence on individuals still needed to be gathered.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: With respect to the first one, he mentioned a concern where he articulated that you go after the company and not the individuals.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: It so happens that in this case, I think if he is referring to the previous case of Keppel O&M, as I had explained in a previous answer in Parliament, that a conditional warning was issued to the company with various penalties.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: And in that case I had also explained that with respect to the individuals, evidence still needed to be gathered and that it was not a case where somebody had got off or not got off.

sections.label: Prosecutorial discretion during term
sections.summary: The passage states that during a prosecutor's term, nobody can interfere with the exercise of his prosecutorial discretion.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: You can take different terms, it depends on various countries.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: But the point I was making, and which is actually the more fundamental point, whatever the term is, during that term, nobody can interfere with that person's exercise of his prosecutorial discretion.

sections.label: 1997 Keppel Corp bribery case
sections.summary: In 1997 Keppel Corp faced 17 bribery charges over $8.3 million paid to an Exxon subsidiary manager, and prosecution proceeded with three charges.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: In 1997, there was another case where Keppel Corp, I do not know the formal legal entity that was involved in this, it does not say Keppel O&M, so I am just reading off what it is.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: It says, "Keppel Corp faced 17 charges of bribery, a total of $8.3 million was paid to the Repair and Technical Manager of a British subsidiary of Exxon" and Keppel got contracts to repair 17 of their tankers. "The statement of facts extended to the court revealed that this had been done with the knowledge and approval of senior Keppel executives and some directors", "the prosecution chose to proceed only with three of the charges.

sections.label: Prosecution disclosure shortcomings
sections.summary: The Leader of the Opposition highlighted shortcomings in the prosecution's duty of disclosure to the defence, as flagged by Court of Appeal judgments.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: In respect of fairness, the Leader of the Opposition has highlighted shortcomings in relation to the prosecution's duty of disclosure to the defence and how prosecutors have fallen short of these duties, as flagged by recent judgments from the Court of Appeal.

sections.label: Criminal legal aid in statute
sections.summary: The passage states criminal legal aid in non-capital cases should be entrenched in statute, not left as a Law Society initiative co-funded by the Government.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: For instance, criminal legal aid provided in non-capital cases should be entrenched in statute and not left as a Law Society initiative albeit co-funded by the Government.

sections.label: Proposals on judicial and AG independence
sections.summary: Dennis Tan suggested State Court Judges not rotate into the Executive and a separate judicial service; Pritam Singh proposed decoupling the Attorney-General's roles.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: MP for Hougang Mr Dennis Tan was concerned about judicial officers at the State Courts and how their independence could be enhanced.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: He suggested the State Court Judges should not be subject to rotation in and out of the Executive Government, and this could be assured by setting up a separate judicial service.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: The Leader of the Opposition Mr Pritam Singh proposed that the Attorney-General's office be subject to structural change to enhance its independence by decoupling the rules of public prosecutor and the Government legal advisor, so that they are held by different people.

sections.label: Government response on fines and defenders
sections.summary: The Minister said the Government would not implement some things, agreed on instalment payments and fine challenges, and is studying a public defender's office.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: On other things, he said the Government would not be implementing them.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: He agreed that the poor do face bigger challenges in paying fines for regulatory offences and the potential snow-balling effect.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: He felt this was a complex issue that required the involvement of many agencies.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: He agreed that instalment payments could be allowed and that he has given directions to look into this.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: The Minister for the said that the Government is at ad idem with MP Pritam Singh and that the Government is consulting stakeholders on the codifying of common law case disclosure requirements.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: Nevertheless, he said that the Government was not fully satisfied with the current system and was looking into the feasibility of setting up a public defender's office.

sections.label: Past shortcomings and government effort
sections.summary: The speaker says he stressed past shortcomings and that the Government keeps working to improve the system and ensure justice for all.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: I think Ms Sylvia Lim said or attributed to me a different formulation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
sentences.text: She appears to have understood my amendments as suggesting that the Government does not admit that there was any shortcoming in the past.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
sentences.text: In fact, if anything, Mr Speaker, the point I was stressing in my speech was that there were shortcomings in the past.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
sentences.text: But the point is, the Government continues to expend effort to improve the system and to ensure there is justice for all.

sentences.speaker: Mr Speaker
sentences.text: The original Motion, as amended, is now before the House.
